screens.title: Why NAT is needed for private subnets
screens.narratorSegment: Many architectures place databases and internal application servers in private subnets to reduce their attack surface. Those resources still need to initiate outbound connections — for example, to download patches, reach external APIs, or fetch container images. Network Address Translation solves this: private instances retain private addresses while outbound traffic appears to originate from a shared public address allocated to the NAT gateway or instance. That allows return traffic for established outbound sessions but prevents unsolicited hosts on the internet from initiating new inbound sessions to your private IPs. A common misconception is that attaching an Internet Gateway to a subnet automatically makes a resource secure; in fact, an Internet Gateway exposes a subnet to two‑way internet traffic if instances have public IPs. NAT preserves the private addressing model for IPv4 and controls inbound exposure. Another important point: IPv6 does not require NAT in the same way because addresses are globally routable. For IPv6, an egress-only Internet Gateway provides a way to let instances make outbound connections while blocking inbound unsolicited traffic. The core takeaway is simple: NAT allows necessary outbound access without giving the internet a path to initiate connections to private resources. When you design your VPC, decide where NAT will sit, how many AZs you will support, and whether managed or self‑managed NAT fits your operational model.

keyIdea.title: NAT purpose
keyIdea.text: NAT enables private instances to start outbound connections while preventing unsolicited inbound connections from the internet.

content.html:
Core Concept NAT purpose
Why NAT matters
NAT lets private instances initiate outbound sessions while preventing unsolicited inbound access from the internet.
Definition
Translate private IPs to a public address for outbound flows; preserve private addressing for internal resources.
Concrete example
A database server without a public IP downloads patches via yum. NAT makes that possible while keeping the server non‑routable from the internet.
Common misconception
Attaching an Internet Gateway to a subnet is not safe for private workloads; NAT or egress‑only IGW patterns are needed for controlled outbound access.
Key Takeaway

Use NAT to enable outbound-only communication for private instances while preventing inbound connections from the public internet.

Annotated flow
A private instance sends a request; the NAT component presents a public address; return traffic flows back through the NAT to the private IP. Routes, security groups, and the NAT device control what flows are allowed.
Why this matters for operations
Choosing between managed and self‑managed NAT affects patching responsibilities, scalability, and availability planning. Plan NAT placement per AZ for resilience.

screens.title: NAT Instance vs NAT Gateway
screens.narratorSegment: There are two main NAT approaches described in this chapter: NAT Instances and NAT Gateways. A NAT Instance is an EC2 instance you configure to perform network address translation. It gives you control: you can run custom software, tune firewall rules, and integrate logging. That control comes with responsibility — you must patch the instance, scale it, and avoid single points of failure by deploying Auto Scaling or additional instances with custom routing. NAT Instances also consume EC2 instance hours and licensing. In contrast, a NAT Gateway is a managed AWS service. AWS handles scaling, patching, and the operational burden. NAT Gateways are highly available within a single Availability Zone, and they scale to handle bursts automatically. The important availability caveat is AZ scope: if the AZ hosting the NAT Gateway fails, private subnets in that AZ lose outbound access unless you deploy NAT Gateways in each AZ and configure private route tables accordingly. A common misconception is that a single NAT Gateway is sufficient for multi‑AZ resilience; for production, create per‑AZ NAT Gateways or alternate designs. Use NAT Instances when you require deep packet inspection or specialized proxy behavior that the managed service cannot provide. For most production workloads, NAT Gateways reduce operational overhead and are the preferred default.

keyIdea.title: Choosing NAT
keyIdea.text: Use NAT Gateways for managed scalability and low operational overhead; use NAT Instances only when custom control or software is required.

content.html:
Comparison NAT Instance vs NAT Gateway
NAT Instance (self‑managed)
  • Full control: install custom agents, proxies, or monitoring.
  • Operational overhead: you must patch, scale, and monitor the instance.
  • Single point of failure unless you design Auto Scaling or multiple instances with route changes.
  • EC2 costs and management overhead apply.
Common mistake
Relying on a single NAT instance in production without scaling or routing for AZ failover.
NAT Gateway (managed)
  • AWS‑managed, auto‑scales to burst traffic and requires no patching from you.
  • Highly available inside an Availability Zone; for multi‑AZ resilience, deploy multiple NAT Gateways.
  • Simpler operational model and recommended for most production workloads.
  • Costs based on gateway hours and data processing, generally simpler than EC2 management.
Pro tip
Create one NAT Gateway per AZ and configure each private subnet to use the NAT in its AZ to avoid cross‑AZ dependencies during failures.

screens.title: Designing NAT for High Availability
screens.narratorSegment: High availability for outbound internet access requires planning NAT placement and route tables across Availability Zones. The recommended pattern is to create a NAT Gateway in each AZ where private subnets exist. Then, configure the private subnets in each AZ to use their AZ’s NAT Gateway by updating the respective route tables. This prevents a single NAT failure from affecting other AZs. A simple two‑AZ design looks like this: public subnet and NAT Gateway in AZ-A and AZ-B, private subnets in each AZ with route tables pointing to the NAT Gateway in their AZ. A common error is to place a single NAT Gateway in one AZ and point all private subnets across AZs to it — this introduces cross‑AZ dependency and a failure domain. During provisioning, remember to allocate an Elastic IP for each NAT Gateway. Also consider cost tradeoffs: multiple NAT Gateways increase managed service costs but lower operational complexity and improve availability. For automation, include NAT Gateway creation and route table associations in your infrastructure templates, ensuring private subnet route tables reference the correct NAT Gateway ID per AZ. Finally, test by simulating AZ failure scenarios if your environment supports it and validate that private instances in unaffected AZs still have outbound access.

keyIdea.title: Per-AZ NAT pattern
keyIdea.text: For resilience, deploy NAT Gateways per AZ and configure private subnet route tables to use the NAT in their AZ to avoid single points of failure.

content.html:
Process Flow High‑availability NAT
Steps to design per‑AZ NAT
  1. Create one public subnet and NAT Gateway in each AZ you use.
  2. Allocate an Elastic IP for each NAT Gateway you create.
  3. Create private subnets in each AZ and a corresponding private route table.
  4. Update each private route table to route 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT Gateway in its AZ.
  5. Automate creation and association in your IaC templates to reduce human error.
Why this matters
Per‑AZ NAT avoids cross‑AZ dependency and reduces the blast radius of an AZ failure.
Example mapping
AZ-A: Public subnet A + NAT Gateway A + Private subnet A route table → NAT GW A. AZ-B: Public subnet B + NAT Gateway B + Private subnet B route table → NAT GW B.
Common mistake
Using one NAT Gateway for multiple AZs without accounting for AZ failover creates a single point of failure for outbound connectivity.
Check your design
Confirm each private subnet’s route table points to the NAT Gateway located in its AZ and plan Elastic IP allocation per NAT.

screens.title: Egress‑only Internet Gateway (IPv6)
screens.narratorSegment: IPv6 addresses are globally routable and therefore IPv6 traffic requires a different approach from IPv4 when you want outbound-only behavior. AWS provides the Egress‑only Internet Gateway for exactly this need: it allows instances with IPv6 addresses in private subnets to initiate outbound connections to the internet while preventing unsolicited inbound IPv6 traffic. Think of it as the IPv6 counterpart to NAT for outbound control in IPv4 private networks. It does not perform NAT; instead, it enforces an egress-only path so responses to outbound requests are allowed back while new incoming sessions are refused. Use this when you have IPv6-only communication requirements or dual-stack networks that must keep IPv6 hosts private. A common misconception is to try to use a NAT Gateway for IPv6; NAT Gateways are for IPv4. Also remember that your IPv6 routing and security groups must be configured to allow outbound flows. The egress-only IGW is a simple, focused component: create it and attach it to your VPC, then add a route for ::/0 in the private subnet’s route table to point to the egress-only gateway. That gives you controlled IPv6 outbound access without exposing hosts to inbound IPv6 connections.

keyIdea.title: Egress-only IGW role
keyIdea.text: Provides outbound-only IPv6 access from private subnets by preventing unsolicited inbound IPv6 connections, without performing NAT.

content.html:
Definition Egress‑only Internet Gateway
What it does
Allows outbound IPv6 traffic from instances in private subnets and prevents unsolicited inbound IPv6 connections.
How to use it
Create an egress-only IGW, then add a route for ::/0 in the private route table that targets the egress-only IGW. Ensure security groups allow outbound IPv6.
Misconception check
Do not confuse this with NAT. IPv6 addresses are globally unique so NAT is not required; the egress-only IGW restricts inbound flows without translating addresses.
Concrete scenario
You have container hosts with IPv6 addresses that need to pull images from an external registry. Use an egress-only IGW to allow the pulls but block inbound IPv6 connections from the internet.
Key takeaway
For IPv6 outbound-only requirements, use an egress-only IGW rather than attempting IPv6 NAT solutions designed for IPv4.

screens.title: VPC Peering fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: VPC Peering creates a direct networking connection between two VPCs so that instances can communicate using private IP addresses as if they were on the same network. This is useful when teams have separate VPCs, or when different environments need to talk privately without crossing the public internet. Peering uses routing: after the connection exists, you must update the route tables in both VPCs to add routes to the peer’s CIDR block that point to the peering connection. A critical characteristic is that peering is non‑transitive. If VPC A peers with VPC B, and VPC B peers with VPC C, VPC A cannot reach VPC C unless A‑C peering is set up separately. This limitation affects network topologies and encourages hub-and-spoke or transit gateway approaches for complex designs. Another important constraint is that peered VPCs cannot have overlapping CIDR blocks; attempting to peer overlapping networks will fail. Security groups and network ACLs still apply across peered connections, so you must ensure both routing and security rules permit the desired traffic. For most straightforward, low-scale inter‑VPC communication, peering is simple and cost effective.

keyIdea.title: Peering essentials
keyIdea.text: VPC Peering enables private VPC-to-VPC connectivity but is non-transitive and requires route table updates and non‑overlapping CIDRs.

content.html:
Core Concept VPC Peering
How peering works
Request a peering connection from one VPC to another, accept the request, then update route tables in both VPCs to route the peer CIDR via the peering connection.
Practical example
You have MyCustomVPC (10.0.0.0/16) and VPC-B (10.10.0.0/16). Create peering, accept, then add routes so each VPC knows how to reach the other’s CIDR.
Design constraints
  • Peering is non‑transitive: you must create direct peering for each pair that needs connectivity.
  • CIDR blocks must not overlap; overlapping CIDRs prevent peering.
  • Remember to update route tables and security groups to allow the traffic you expect.
Misconception check
Do not assume peering will transit other peering links; peering requires explicit bilateral connections.

screens.title: VPC Peering: request, accept, and route
screens.narratorSegment: Creating and validating a VPC peering connection is a straightforward process with a few critical steps to get right. First, issue a create‑vpc‑peering‑connection request from one VPC to the peer VPC and note the peering ID. From the peer VPC’s account, accept the peering connection. After acceptance, add route table entries in both VPCs: add a route for the peer CIDR that points to the peering connection ID. Common mistakes include adding the route only in one VPC or forgetting to update security groups to permit the new peer traffic. If you launch instances to test connectivity, confirm that security groups allow the protocol you’re testing, for example ICMP for ping. Overlapping CIDRs will block peering, and peering does not automatically create DNS resolution across VPCs — if you need private DNS resolution, plan for it separately. A simple validation sequence is: launch instances in each VPC, open the necessary security group ports, ping the peer private IP, and observe connectivity. If ping fails, check route tables, peering acceptance status, CIDR overlap, and security groups in that order. This checklist reduces the most common setup mistakes.

keyIdea.title: Peering checklist
keyIdea.text: Create and accept the peering, add routes in both VPCs, ensure non-overlapping CIDRs, and permit traffic in security groups to validate connectivity.

content.html:
Process Flow Peering steps
CLI sequence (summary)
# Create peering (from VPC-A)
aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-id <YourVpcId> --peer-vpc-id <VpcId-B> --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=vpc-peering-connection,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=VPC-A-to-B-Peering}]'

# Accept peering (from VPC-B)
aws ec2 accept-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-peering-connection-id <VpcPeeringConnectionId>

# Add route in VPC-A route table
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id <MyPublicRouteTableId> --destination-cidr-block 10.10.0.0/16 --vpc-peering-connection-id <VpcPeeringConnectionId>

# Add route in VPC-B route table
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id <RouteTableId-B> --destination-cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 --vpc-peering-connection-id <VpcPeeringConnectionId>
Validation & pitfalls
  • Test connectivity with ping or the actual protocol; open security groups accordingly.
  • Check peering status is active; routing is configured in both VPCs.
  • Remember peering is not transitive and CIDR blocks must not overlap.
Tip
Automate route updates and acceptance procedures to reduce manual errors when creating peering between accounts.

screens.title: VPC Endpoints: Gateway and Interface
screens.narratorSegment: VPC Endpoints let your VPC access supported AWS services privately, keeping traffic inside the AWS network and avoiding the public internet. There are two types: Gateway Endpoints and Interface Endpoints. Gateway Endpoints are route table targets and are available for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB. You create a gateway endpoint and add route table entries so traffic to those services is routed directly without needing an Internet Gateway, NAT, or VPN. Gateway Endpoints are free to use. Interface Endpoints are powered by AWS PrivateLink and create Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs) in your subnets with private IP addresses. They support many AWS services beyond S3 and DynamoDB, and also third‑party or partner services available via PrivateLink. Interface Endpoints incur charges for endpoint hours and data processing. The security benefit is strong: endpoint traffic never traverses the internet, reducing exposure and often reducing data transfer costs. A common design consideration is costs versus coverage: use gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB when possible and interface endpoints for other services requiring private IP connectivity. Configure policies and security groups on interface endpoints to control access, and update route tables when using gateway endpoints so the traffic flows as expected.

content.html:
Core Concept VPC Endpoints
Gateway Endpoint
Route table target used for S3 and DynamoDB. Add a route for the service and traffic stays inside AWS. No endpoint hours or data processing charges.
Use case
Private instances need to access S3 for backups or data retrieval without using NAT or the internet.
Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink)
Creates ENIs in your subnet and exposes a private IP for the service. Supports many AWS and partner services but incurs endpoint hours and data processing charges.
Security considerations
Use security groups and endpoint policies to control which principals and subnets can access the endpoint.
Key Takeaway
Choose gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB when possible for cost and simplicity; use interface endpoints for other services that require PrivateLink connectivity.

screens.title: Gateway vs Interface Endpoints — decisions and costs
screens.narratorSegment: When deciding between gateway and interface endpoints, consider supported services, cost model, and operational controls. Gateway endpoints are purpose-built for S3 and DynamoDB and act as a route table target. They are free and scale without you managing ENIs. Use a gateway endpoint when the traffic pattern is service access from many instances and you want a cost‑effective solution. Interface endpoints use PrivateLink, creating ENIs in subnets with private IPs. They support a broader set of services and partner integrations but charge for endpoint hours and data processing. Interface endpoints are useful when you need endpoint-level security via security groups, or when you need a private IP address in a subnet to reach the service. Both improve security by keeping traffic inside AWS and can reduce data transfer costs compared to internet routing. A common operational trap is misconfiguring route tables for gateway endpoints or forgetting security group rules on interface endpoints. Also consider service quotas and ENI limits when you deploy many interface endpoints. For most S3 traffic, gateway endpoints are the simplest and cheapest pattern; for other services or private integrations, interface endpoints are the right choice.

Comparison Gateway vs Interface
Gateway Endpoint

  • Route table target; no ENIs required.
  • No endpoint hours or data processing charges.
  • Best for high-volume S3 access from private subnets.
Interface Endpoint

  • Supports many AWS services and partner services.
  • Charges for endpoint hours and data processing apply.
  • Use when you need private IPs, security groups, or partner integrations.
Operational note
Remember ENI limits and design your subnets and quotas to accommodate interface endpoints at scale. For S3, prefer gateway endpoints whenever possible for simplicity and cost.

screens.title: Hands‑on: Create Private Subnet + NAT Gateway and Peer VPCs
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough guides you through the exact CLI steps to create a private subnet, allocate an Elastic IP, create a NAT Gateway, update a private route table, and then create a second VPC and peer it with your primary VPC. Follow the commands and keep track of resource IDs for route updates. First, create a private subnet in your existing VPC and note the SubnetId. Then allocate an Elastic IP and create a NAT Gateway in a public subnet. Once the NAT Gateway is available, create or use a private route table and add a default route that points to the NAT Gateway so that private subnet traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 flows through the NAT. Launch an EC2 instance into the private subnet with no public IP, use a bastion host to SSH into it, and verify outbound connectivity with a package update or ping. For VPC peering, create a second VPC and subnet, request a peering connection from the first VPC, accept it from the second, and add routes in both VPC route tables so each can reach the other’s CIDR. Test by pinging a private IP across the peered VPCs. Remember to check security groups and avoid CIDR overlap. These steps map directly to the chapter’s lab scenario and validate the networking patterns we discussed.

keyIdea.title: Lab objective
keyIdea.text: Create a private subnet with NAT-based outbound access and establish VPC peering, then verify connectivity using a bastion host and private pings.

content.html:
Hands‑On Activity Private subnet with NAT & Peering
Part 1 — NAT Gateway
# Create a private subnet
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id <YourVpcId> --cidr-block 10.0.2.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1b --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=MyPrivateSubnet}]'

# Allocate an Elastic IP for the NAT Gateway
aws ec2 allocate-address --domain vpc --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=elastic-ip,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=MyNATGatewayEIP}]'

# Create a NAT Gateway in the public subnet
aws ec2 create-nat-gateway --subnet-id <YourPublicSubnetId> --allocation-id <YourElasticIpAllocationId> --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=natgateway,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=MyNATGateway}]'

# Create a route table for the private subnet
aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id <YourVpcId> --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=route-table,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=MyPrivateRouteTable}]'

# Add a default route to the NAT Gateway
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id <MyPrivateRouteTableId> --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --nat-gateway-id <YourNatGatewayId>

# Associate the route table with the private subnet
aws ec2 associate-route-table --subnet-id <MyPrivateSubnetId> --route-table-id <MyPrivateRouteTableId>
Part 2 — VPC Peering
# Create a second VPC and subnet (VPC-B)
aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.10.0.0/16 --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=vpc,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=VPC-B}]'
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id <VpcId-B> --cidr-block 10.10.1.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1a --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=VPC-B-Subnet}]'

# Request peering from VPC-A to VPC-B
aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-id <YourVpcId> --peer-vpc-id <VpcId-B> --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=vpc-peering-connection,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=VPC-A-to-B-Peering}]'

# Accept the peering (from VPC-B account)
aws ec2 accept-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-peering-connection-id <YourVpcPeeringConnectionId>

# Update route tables in both VPCs to add the peer CIDR via the peering connection
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id <MyPublicRouteTableId> --destination-cidr-block 10.10.0.0/16 --vpc-peering-connection-id <YourVpcPeeringConnectionId>
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id <RouteTableId-B> --destination-cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 --vpc-peering-connection-id <YourVpcPeeringConnectionId>
Verification
Launch instances in each VPC, ensure security groups permit ICMP or the desired protocol, and ping the private IP across peered VPCs to validate connectivity.

screens.title: On‑prem connectivity: Site‑to‑Site VPN
screens.narratorSegment: Site‑to‑Site VPN provides an encrypted connection over the public internet between your on‑premises network and your AWS VPC. It’s a cost‑effective option for hybrid architectures, especially for development, testing, or smaller offices that require secure connectivity but do not need the throughput or latency guarantees of a dedicated link. The AWS side is typically a Virtual Private Gateway attached to the VPC, and the on‑premises side is represented by a Customer Gateway that points to your VPN device. For higher availability, AWS recommends configuring two VPN tunnels from your Customer Gateway to the Virtual Private Gateway so that a tunnel failure does not sever connectivity. Site‑to‑Site VPNs are straightforward to set up and are encrypted, but because they traverse the public internet, they do not offer the same consistency of latency and throughput as dedicated circuits. A common reasoning error is to assume VPN provides predictable latency equal to Direct Connect; it does not. Use VPN when encryption across the internet is acceptable, budget constraints exist, or when you need a quick hybrid connection before committing to a Direct Connect link.

content.html:
Architecture Site‑to‑Site VPN
How it’s built
Customer Gateway represents your on‑prem device; Virtual Private Gateway attaches to the VPC. Two tunnels recommended for redundancy. Traffic is encrypted over the internet.
Use cases
Development/test environments, backup connectivity, or smaller remote offices that require secure access to VPC resources.
Operational notes
  • Configure two tunnels for high availability.
  • Monitor tunnel health and plan for failover in routing.
  • Expect variable latency and throughput since the internet is used.
Misconception check
Do not expect Direct Connect performance from a VPN. Use VPN for secure, flexible connectivity where dedicated performance is not required.

screens.title: AWS Direct Connect
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Direct Connect provides a dedicated, private network connection from your premises to an AWS Direct Connect location. Unlike Site‑to‑Site VPN, Direct Connect bypasses the public internet, delivering more consistent performance, lower latency, and predictable bandwidth. This makes it the right choice for mission‑critical workloads, large data transfers, or cases where consistent network performance matters for user experience or regulatory reasons. Direct Connect typically requires more planning and cost: provisioning circuits, arranging cross‑connects at a carrier‑neutral location, and configuring virtual interfaces to connect to your VPCs. It can also reduce data transfer costs for high volumes. Some organizations use a hybrid approach: Direct Connect for production traffic and VPN for backup or less critical links. A practical pitfall to plan for is redundancy: use multiple Direct Connect connections or pair Direct Connect with a VPN failover to maintain connectivity if a circuit fails. In short, choose Direct Connect when you need dedicated performance and are ready to invest in circuit provisioning and redundancy planning. AWS Direct Connect means direct connect is a dedicated connection that bypasses the internet for consistent performance; best for high-volume or latency-sensitive workloads.. In practical terms, dedicated private network connections for consistent performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Architecture Direct Connect
What Direct Connect gives you
A private, dedicated circuit into AWS. Predictable bandwidth, lower latency, and potential cost savings on large data transfers.
When to choose it
Enterprise workloads with high bandwidth needs, consistent latency requirements, or regulatory constraints requiring private connectivity.
Redundancy and planning
  • Provision multiple Direct Connect connections for redundancy or pair Direct Connect with VPN as a backup.
  • Plan cross‑connects and carrier relationships; provisioning times are longer than for VPN.
  • Consider virtual interfaces and routing to your VPCs and on‑prem networks.
Key takeaway
Use Direct Connect when you need predictable, private network performance and are prepared to invest in circuit provisioning and redundancy.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you’ll learn how to let private resources communicate outward without becoming publicly reachable, connect VPCs privately, and link your on‑premises network to AWS in a secure, reliable way. We start by making the common design decision: when a server in a private subnet needs updates or A P I access, how do you let it initiate outbound connections while preventing unsolicited inbound traffic? You’ll compare self‑managed NAT Instances with managed NAT Gateways and learn availability patterns for multi‑AZ deployments. Then we’ll cover IPv6 needs and the Egress‑only Internet Gateway, which protects against unsolicited inbound IPv6 connections. You’ll also learn VPC Peering basics and a crucial constraint: peering is not transitive, so designs that assume transit will fail. Next, we’ll examine VPC Endpoints — gateway and interface types — that let your VPC reach AWS services privately. Finally, you’ll learn on‑premises options: Site‑to‑Site VPN for encrypted internet tunnels and Direct Connect for dedicated private links with consistent performance. Throughout, you’ll see concrete CLI steps and a hands‑on lab scenario to create a private subnet with a NAT Gateway and a VPC peering connection so you can practise these patterns safely.

By the end of this chapter you will compare NAT Gateways and NAT Instances so you can choose an appropriate outbound pattern, explain egress‑only gateways for IPv6, design and implement VPC Peering, and understand VPC Endpoint types to route traffic to AWS services privately. These are practical skills: for example, identifying when to use a managed NAT Gateway instead of a self‑managed NAT Instance can reduce operational overhead and improve availability. You will also learn to update route tables correctly and avoid common mistakes like overlapping CIDR blocks when peering. Together, these objectives map to design decisions you will make when building production VPC networks and hybrid connections. Each objective is measurable: you will create a private subnet that can reach the internet outbound-only, configure an egress-only gateway for IPv6 traffic, establish a peering connection and verify routing, and choose and configure the correct VPC endpoint type for S3 or another service. These skills help you maintain secure, predictable connectivity for applications that must access external resources without exposing themselves to inbound internet traffic.

This second objectives slide focuses on measurable, hands‑on outcomes you will complete. You will create a private subnet and provision a NAT Gateway, allocate an Elastic IP, and associate a private route table so instances can initiate outbound connections for updates. You will practice creating a second VPC, request and accept a VPC peering connection, and then add routes in both VPCs to verify connectivity. You will also configure a gateway endpoint for S3 or DynamoDB, and demonstrate an interface endpoint for another service, learning why gateway endpoints are free and route‑table based while interface endpoints use ENIs and incur charges. Finally, you will prepare a simple Site‑to‑Site VPN connection and understand when Direct Connect is a more appropriate option for performance and cost at scale. Each objective includes a short verification step: ping or curl for outbound access, and a controlled ping across peered VPCs, and checking that endpoint traffic remains within the AWS network. These verification steps make the competencies demonstrable and repeatable.

Many architectures place databases and internal application servers in private subnets to reduce their attack surface. Those resources still need to initiate outbound connections — for example, to download patches, reach external APIs, or fetch container images. Network Address Translation solves this: private instances retain private addresses while outbound traffic appears to originate from a shared public address allocated to the NAT gateway or instance. That allows return traffic for established outbound sessions but prevents unsolicited hosts on the internet from initiating new inbound sessions to your private IPs. A common misconception is that attaching an Internet Gateway to a subnet automatically makes a resource secure; in fact, an Internet Gateway exposes a subnet to two‑way internet traffic if instances have public IPs. NAT preserves the private addressing model for IPv4 and controls inbound exposure. Another important point: IPv6 does not require NAT in the same way because addresses are globally routable. For IPv6, an egress-only Internet Gateway provides a way to let instances make outbound connections while blocking inbound unsolicited traffic. The core takeaway is simple: NAT allows necessary outbound access without giving the internet a path to initiate connections to private resources. When you design your VPC, decide where NAT will sit, how many AZs you will support, and whether managed or self‑managed NAT fits your operational model.

There are two main NAT approaches described in this chapter: NAT Instances and NAT Gateways. A NAT Instance is an EC2 instance you configure to perform network address translation. It gives you control: you can run custom software, tune firewall rules, and integrate logging. That control comes with responsibility — you must patch the instance, scale it, and avoid single points of failure by deploying Auto Scaling or additional instances with custom routing. NAT Instances also consume EC2 instance hours and licensing. In contrast, a NAT Gateway is a managed AWS service. AWS handles scaling, patching, and the operational burden. NAT Gateways are highly available within a single Availability Zone, and they scale to handle bursts automatically. The important availability caveat is AZ scope: if the AZ hosting the NAT Gateway fails, private subnets in that AZ lose outbound access unless you deploy NAT Gateways in each AZ and configure private route tables accordingly. A common misconception is that a single NAT Gateway is sufficient for multi‑AZ resilience; for production, create per‑AZ NAT Gateways or alternate designs. Use NAT Instances when you require deep packet inspection or specialized proxy behavior that the managed service cannot provide. For most production workloads, NAT Gateways reduce operational overhead and are the preferred default.

High availability for outbound internet access requires planning NAT placement and route tables across Availability Zones. The recommended pattern is to create a NAT Gateway in each AZ where private subnets exist. Then, configure the private subnets in each AZ to use their AZ’s NAT Gateway by updating the respective route tables. This prevents a single NAT failure from affecting other AZs. A simple two‑AZ design looks like this: public subnet and NAT Gateway in AZ-A and AZ-B, private subnets in each AZ with route tables pointing to the NAT Gateway in their AZ. A common error is to place a single NAT Gateway in one AZ and point all private subnets across AZs to it — this introduces cross‑AZ dependency and a failure domain. During provisioning, remember to allocate an Elastic IP for each NAT Gateway. Also consider cost tradeoffs: multiple NAT Gateways increase managed service costs but lower operational complexity and improve availability. For automation, include NAT Gateway creation and route table associations in your infrastructure templates, ensuring private subnet route tables reference the correct NAT Gateway ID per AZ. Finally, test by simulating AZ failure scenarios if your environment supports it and validate that private instances in unaffected AZs still have outbound access.

IPv6 addresses are globally routable and therefore IPv6 traffic requires a different approach from IPv4 when you want outbound-only behavior. AWS provides the Egress‑only Internet Gateway for exactly this need: it allows instances with IPv6 addresses in private subnets to initiate outbound connections to the internet while preventing unsolicited inbound IPv6 traffic. Think of it as the IPv6 counterpart to NAT for outbound control in IPv4 private networks. It does not perform NAT; instead, it enforces an egress-only path so responses to outbound requests are allowed back while new incoming sessions are refused. Use this when you have IPv6-only communication requirements or dual-stack networks that must keep IPv6 hosts private. A common misconception is to try to use a NAT Gateway for IPv6; NAT Gateways are for IPv4. Also remember that your IPv6 routing and security groups must be configured to allow outbound flows. The egress-only IGW is a simple, focused component: create it and attach it to your VPC, then add a route for ::/0 in the private subnet’s route table to point to the egress-only gateway. That gives you controlled IPv6 outbound access without exposing hosts to inbound IPv6 connections.

VPC Peering creates a direct networking connection between two VPCs so that instances can communicate using private IP addresses as if they were on the same network. This is useful when teams have separate VPCs, or when different environments need to talk privately without crossing the public internet. Peering uses routing: after the connection exists, you must update the route tables in both VPCs to add routes to the peer’s CIDR block that point to the peering connection. A critical characteristic is that peering is non‑transitive. If VPC A peers with VPC B, and VPC B peers with VPC C, VPC A cannot reach VPC C unless A‑C peering is set up separately. This limitation affects network topologies and encourages hub-and-spoke or transit gateway approaches for complex designs. Another important constraint is that peered VPCs cannot have overlapping CIDR blocks; attempting to peer overlapping networks will fail. Security groups and network ACLs still apply across peered connections, so you must ensure both routing and security rules permit the desired traffic. For most straightforward, low-scale inter‑VPC communication, peering is simple and cost effective.

Creating and validating a VPC peering connection is a straightforward process with a few critical steps to get right. First, issue a create‑vpc‑peering‑connection request from one VPC to the peer VPC and note the peering ID. From the peer VPC’s account, accept the peering connection. After acceptance, add route table entries in both VPCs: add a route for the peer CIDR that points to the peering connection ID. Common mistakes include adding the route only in one VPC or forgetting to update security groups to permit the new peer traffic. If you launch instances to test connectivity, confirm that security groups allow the protocol you’re testing, for example ICMP for ping. Overlapping CIDRs will block peering, and peering does not automatically create DNS resolution across VPCs — if you need private DNS resolution, plan for it separately. A simple validation sequence is: launch instances in each VPC, open the necessary security group ports, ping the peer private IP, and observe connectivity. If ping fails, check route tables, peering acceptance status, CIDR overlap, and security groups in that order. This checklist reduces the most common setup mistakes.

VPC Endpoints let your VPC access supported AWS services privately, keeping traffic inside the AWS network and avoiding the public internet. There are two types: Gateway Endpoints and Interface Endpoints. Gateway Endpoints are route table targets and are available for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB. You create a gateway endpoint and add route table entries so traffic to those services is routed directly without needing an Internet Gateway, NAT, or VPN. Gateway Endpoints are free to use. Interface Endpoints are powered by AWS PrivateLink and create Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs) in your subnets with private IP addresses. They support many AWS services beyond S3 and DynamoDB, and also third‑party or partner services available via PrivateLink. Interface Endpoints incur charges for endpoint hours and data processing. The security benefit is strong: endpoint traffic never traverses the internet, reducing exposure and often reducing data transfer costs. A common design consideration is costs versus coverage: use gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB when possible and interface endpoints for other services requiring private IP connectivity. Configure policies and security groups on interface endpoints to control access, and update route tables when using gateway endpoints so the traffic flows as expected.

When deciding between gateway and interface endpoints, consider supported services, cost model, and operational controls. Gateway endpoints are purpose-built for S3 and DynamoDB and act as a route table target. They are free and scale without you managing ENIs. Use a gateway endpoint when the traffic pattern is service access from many instances and you want a cost‑effective solution. Interface endpoints use PrivateLink, creating ENIs in subnets with private IPs. They support a broader set of services and partner integrations but charge for endpoint hours and data processing. Interface endpoints are useful when you need endpoint-level security via security groups, or when you need a private IP address in a subnet to reach the service. Both improve security by keeping traffic inside AWS and can reduce data transfer costs compared to internet routing. A common operational trap is misconfiguring route tables for gateway endpoints or forgetting security group rules on interface endpoints. Also consider service quotas and ENI limits when you deploy many interface endpoints. For most S3 traffic, gateway endpoints are the simplest and cheapest pattern; for other services or private integrations, interface endpoints are the right choice.

This walkthrough guides you through the exact CLI steps to create a private subnet, allocate an Elastic IP, create a NAT Gateway, update a private route table, and then create a second VPC and peer it with your primary VPC. Follow the commands and keep track of resource IDs for route updates. First, create a private subnet in your existing VPC and note the SubnetId. Then allocate an Elastic IP and create a NAT Gateway in a public subnet. Once the NAT Gateway is available, create or use a private route table and add a default route that points to the NAT Gateway so that private subnet traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 flows through the NAT. Launch an EC2 instance into the private subnet with no public IP, use a bastion host to SSH into it, and verify outbound connectivity with a package update or ping. For VPC peering, create a second VPC and subnet, request a peering connection from the first VPC, accept it from the second, and add routes in both VPC route tables so each can reach the other’s CIDR. Test by pinging a private IP across the peered VPCs. Remember to check security groups and avoid CIDR overlap. These steps map directly to the chapter’s lab scenario and validate the networking patterns we discussed.

Site‑to‑Site VPN provides an encrypted connection over the public internet between your on‑premises network and your AWS VPC. It’s a cost‑effective option for hybrid architectures, especially for development, testing, or smaller offices that require secure connectivity but do not need the throughput or latency guarantees of a dedicated link. The AWS side is typically a Virtual Private Gateway attached to the VPC, and the on‑premises side is represented by a Customer Gateway that points to your VPN device. For higher availability, AWS recommends configuring two VPN tunnels from your Customer Gateway to the Virtual Private Gateway so that a tunnel failure does not sever connectivity. Site‑to‑Site VPNs are straightforward to set up and are encrypted, but because they traverse the public internet, they do not offer the same consistency of latency and throughput as dedicated circuits. A common reasoning error is to assume VPN provides predictable latency equal to Direct Connect; it does not. Use VPN when encryption across the internet is acceptable, budget constraints exist, or when you need a quick hybrid connection before committing to a Direct Connect link.

AWS Direct Connect provides a dedicated, private network connection from your premises to an AWS Direct Connect location. Unlike Site‑to‑Site VPN, Direct Connect bypasses the public internet, delivering more consistent performance, lower latency, and predictable bandwidth. This makes it the right choice for mission‑critical workloads, large data transfers, or cases where consistent network performance matters for user experience or regulatory reasons. Direct Connect typically requires more planning and cost: provisioning circuits, arranging cross‑connects at a carrier‑neutral location, and configuring virtual interfaces to connect to your VPCs. It can also reduce data transfer costs for high volumes. Some organizations use a hybrid approach: Direct Connect for production traffic and VPN for backup or less critical links. A practical pitfall to plan for is redundancy: use multiple Direct Connect connections or pair Direct Connect with a VPN failover to maintain connectivity if a circuit fails. In short, choose Direct Connect when you need dedicated performance and are ready to invest in circuit provisioning and redundancy planning. AWS Direct Connect means direct connect is a dedicated connection that bypasses the internet for consistent performance; best for high-volume or latency-sensitive workloads.. In practical terms, dedicated private network connections for consistent performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

These are the core terms you should remember and how they relate to design decisions. A NAT Gateway is a managed service that enables instances in private subnets to initiate outbound IPv4 traffic while preventing unsolicited inbound connections; it is resilient and auto‑scales within an AZ. A NAT Instance is a self‑managed EC2 instance that performs NAT and provides greater control but requires you to manage patching, scaling, and high availability. An Egress‑only Internet Gateway allows IPv6 hosts to make outbound connections while preventing inbound IPv6 traffic, offering the IPv6 outbound-only counterpart to NAT for IPv4. Keep these definitions in mind when mapping security requirements to connectivity patterns and availability needs. Finish by remembering VPC Peering, VPC Endpoints, Site‑to‑Site VPN, and Direct Connect. VPC Peering connects two VPCs privately using route table entries but is non‑transitive and requires direct peering for each pair. VPC Endpoints let your VPC privately reach AWS services: gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB are route-based and free, whereas interface endpoints use ENIs and PrivateLink and incur charges. For hybrid connectivity, Site‑to‑Site VPN provides encrypted tunnels over the internet and is quick to set up, while Direct Connect offers dedicated circuits for predictable performance and lower costs at scale. When you design networks, balance control, cost, and availability: choose peering for simple inter‑VPC links, endpoints for private service access, VPN for flexible encrypted links, and Direct Connect for performance‑sensitive, high‑volume traffic.
